Marikana 2015

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
THree years, 45 000 pages of testimony, will the marikana report reveal the truth

Further information:
Proposal Marikana 2015

12th August 2012 – a day that changed South Africa forever. The day a democratic South Africa’s police service, shot and killed 34 Lonmin miners striking for R12500 per month.

Its also a day that changed hundreds of lives of fathers, wives, children, parents, brothers and sisters. Suicides, heart attacks, divorce, many of the families on both sides of the conflict have walked through the shadows of depression and despair.

A day after what has been called a massacre, an execution, a shocked president cut short his SADC meeting in Zimbabwe, and on his return declared a commission of enquiry to establish exactly what happened.

For three long years the commission has lumbered on, interest in its work began to wane except on days when the big guns had to answer the tough questions. In November last year it finally wrapped up its work – 45 000 pages and hundreds of millions of rands later, the report is about to be released.
But what will it find? Will Police Commissioner Riah Phiyega face the axe or worse, face charges; will Deputy President Cyril Ramaphosa be censured for his role in the tragic events that unfolded. And what of Lonmin, the company worth R12 billion rand now worth less than the cost of sinking a single mine shaft at around R3 billion?

The police have always claimed that they shot muti crazed miners in self defence. But is that really the case? We speak to Head of litigation at SERI Nomzamo Zondo who tells us what happened that day and how it impacted on the families of the miners shot.

We speak to widows Zameka Nungu, Ntombizolile Mosebatsana and Nandipha Yona about their loss and how their only option for survival was to take jobs at the company that they believe were complicit in their husbands deaths.

But while the shattered lives of the miners widows has received much media attention, the police on the frontlines have also paid a price. Salmon Vermaak air commander in the chopper on the day defied the police and refused to doctor his evidence. His story has ended in divorce and PTSD. A similar story is told by former Capt of the Tactical Response team Paul Loest a burly career policeman who says Marikana was a tragedy that should never have happened.

Press Release:


Marikana Remains
This week president Zuma let slip his controversial take on the 2012 killing of 34 mineworkers saying that the police were ‘stopping violence’. The nation has patiently waited for the release of the delayed Marikana report, promised by end June. Did the police act in self-defence against muti-crazed miners or could the massacre have been avoided? Carte Blanche speaks to former SAPS commanders who were on the scene and the widows of the miners who were killed.


Script:


Marikana Report 2015 Final script TX Sunday 28th June

Ntombizolile Mosebatsane
Its here, the first bullet -The second one is here – two gunshots to the head

Commentary One
August 16th 2012 –the day our young democracy lost its innocence.
Marikana chalks up another notch in our violent history.

Ntombizolile
I was very sad …

Commentary Two
Zameka Nungu and Ntombizolile Mosebatsane were destitute and begged Lonmin for jobs. Now they both work at Marikana mine as cleaners.

Devi
Zameka how many times was Jackson shot?
Zameka
Eleven bullets. This side here on the leg- his entire leg was bullet riddled

Commentary Three
There were 44 deaths that dreadful August- 34 striking miners gunned down by police, yet the collateral damage has shattered many more lives. Tanya khun’s husband Danie was one of the first to open fire that day

Tanya
It would have been better if my husband had died because then I could have really got the chance to mourn him

Commentary Four
Soon afterwards he suffered epileptic seizures and he can no longer work.

Tanya
But now the man I have been given back is somebody I have to learn to love again

Commentary five
Widow Nandipha Yona also left her home in the Eastern Cape to work at Marikana.


Nandipha Yona
The way I see it the truth will not be revealed.

LINK
The truth? Would the Farlam commission negotiate its way through the lies and omissions to find it? Well on Thursday after two years and thousands of pages of testimony the President finally released the report

PRESIDENT ZUMA
The commission has also recommended that there must be an enquiry into the fitness to hold office of the national police commissioner

Commentary six
Political analyst professor Tinyiko Maluleke shared his concerns

Tinyiko Maluleke
The Government is totally innocent as far as Marikana – all of them had nothing to do with this it was just the police – now seriously no one can believe that and I think that is the problem, that is a real problem.

Commentary seven
But what he found equally shocking was the absence of the widows. They weren’t even informed about the reports release

Tinyiko Maluleke
They represent all of us. Them being absent spoke more than volumes and volumes of pages

Commentary eight
Many of those 600 pages concern the actions of the police – in particular Police commissioner Riah Phiyega- found by the commission unfit to hold office

Tinyiko Maluleke
I hope she doesn’t wait to be fired. Her situation has become untenable – the police wont respect her, her political principles have abandoned her

Commentary nine
The commission found that she deliberately tried to conceal a meeting the night before the massacre where a crucial decision to use lethal force to end the strike, ultimately led to the bloodshed

Nomzamo Zondo
We spent four months on Riah Piyegha, who knew nothing, saw nothing, who wasn’t even there

Commentary ten
Nomzamo Zondo is the Head of Litigation at the Socio- economic rights institute. They represent the families and AMCU

Devi
In your final heads of argument what are you asking for?

Nomzamo Zondo
We ask for the criminal prosecution of all the commanders especially Calitz who gave the order, we ask for the criminal prosecution of those at Lonmin who called the police, we also ask for the compensation for the families.

Commentary eleven
But a lack of compensation is one of the disappointments coming out of the report

Tinyiko
Once again the poor widows have to go and start the fight from scratch and institute the civil suits at their own costs

Commentary twelve
But if the commission was silent on compensation, they were vocal about the actions of the police. Commanders can expect criminal investigations.

Paul
We were placed in a very difficult and an impossible situation and I am not sure who created that situation for us, that was my job – if you are told to do a certain thing you do it.

Commentary thirteen
Paul Loest was commander of the tactical response team on the day.

Paul
I specifically said to my members that if these miners approach us and they stop 2 meters in front of us then we will just stand and wait it out.

Derek
Was the order ever given to open fire?
No.
Derek
Paul
Never
Paul
We were instructed that if the members felt that their life was threatened then they can act in self defence

Commentary Fourteen
Even to the lay-person it seems like a crazy idea for the tactical response team who are trained to use lethal force to do crowd control.

LINK
And the commission found that the Public order police units who should have been better deployed, need a major overhaul.

Derek
Should you have been involved from the start?

Paul
During an operation like Marikana there must always be a tactical element…in hindsight, no it probably was not the correct thing to do

LINK
The commission found that it would have been impossible to disarm and disperse the strikers on that day without significant bloodshed- but the police had been warned – by one of their own

Salmon
In the first place it was a stupid idea to approach the big crowd of 3000 and try to disarm them at 3 o clock in the afternoon. How long before it gets dark
Derek
So you are saying it was a plan that was going to end in bloodshed
Salmon
I foresee that and I warned them

Commentary fifteen
Salmon Vermaak was the air commander on that day, the police’s eye in the sky, taking photographs. At the commission he stood up and defied the police version of events.


Salmon
I saw that they were trying to change the timelines on my photos, and I said if you are going to change the time lines I will open a case of fraud against you

Commentary Sixteen
The police dropped him as a witness – but he told his story finally anyway. It was a decision that cost him dearly

Salmon
I have paid a price to stand up for the truth. I have lost my career
Derek
What about your family?
Salmon
It had a huge impact on them .. …he starts to cry …
Derek
Sorry Salmon
Salmon
In the end my marriage ended
Derek
And Marikana was the last straw
Salmon nods.
Up sound

Cease fire! Cease fire!

Paul
I did everything I could possibly have done, as soon as the dust settled immediately, I shouted ceasefire

Commentary seventeen
Paul is another casualty of Marikana. He’s also been criticized for not calling ambulances sooner. Now, medically boarded with post traumatic stress – his career and his marriage have both ended

Paul
Death has a smell and that is the smell I got and it triggered a huge amount of flashbacks and I had to compose myself because I was the commander

LINK
After the first 17 miners were gunned down its hard to understand why no one called a halt to the entire operation. Instead the police hunted down the other miners right here.

Commentary eighteen
Its here that Ntombizolile’s husband Thabiso was shot twice in the head

Ntombizolile Mosebatsane
I was thinking the commission would give some answers and even the truth / and then it get into the end but I didn’t find the truth of what happened at scene two

Commentary nineteen
The commission found there was a complete lack of command and control at scene two

Nomzamo Zondo
Marikana was never about self defence, because if Marikana was about self defence scene two would never have happened

Commentary twenty
Much of the blame for the deaths is leveled at former non- executive director of Lonmin, Cyril Ramaphosa whose calls and e mails ensured droves of police arrived on the scene.

Tinyiko
He gets a clean bill – I think its one thing for the commission to find him clean its quite another for the public perceptions and I think in the eye of the public that e mail that he wrote and the phone calls he made to the minister will haunt him for a long time

Commentary twenty- one
In the boardrooms of Lonmin, they are studying the report while keeping an eye on their falling share price, while in the hostels the widows, once again feel betrayed.

Ntombizolile
I am going to tell my kids that your father was brutally killed by the SAPS under the government of the ANC

THE END
